chapter_title: Concerning why if a [Nail] is cut the Person shall
spiritual_reading:
# Spiritual Translation

## ¶2

Why is it that when essential faculties are severed from the natural mind of a person, that person suffers spiritual pain? Yet if the outermost external knowledges upon the governing principle of the mind are stripped away, and the most external natural forms of one's power and one's lowest natural life are removed, one does not perceive their loss [GAP-1: ...] Some of these outermost things even now regenerate an[GAP-2: d ...] again. Just as the most external natural forms [GAP-3: ...] so the outermost knowledges shall be restored and [GAP-4: ...] sever a particular faculty of power, one in [GAP-5: ...] upon the essential faculties of the [natural mi]nd that you [GAP-6: ...] him [GAP-7: ...] since this stage of life to the [GAP-8: ...] the external mind ag[a]in.

*The teaching here distinguishes between what is ultimate and replaceable in the natural mind — mere outward forms of knowledge and the lowest natural coverings — and what constitutes an essential living faculty. The outermost things, being merely terminal forms, regenerate after removal because their spiritual root remains intact. But the deeper faculties, once destroyed, occasion real spiritual suffering because they participate in the interior life itself.*

## ¶5

Th[at the] natural mind is like the ground of reception, wh[ile these] essential faculties als[GAP-9: o ...] of it are like the perceptions rooted therein. There are varieties [GAP-10: ...] of perception one shall find growing in the natural mind. They aris[e] and are restored again and stand firm in the understanding. They have not [GAP-11: ...] Again, there are other perceptions that if they are destroyed shall not [GAP-12: be restored ...] and they grow, as they are li[GAP-13: ke ...] which shall be cut off and yet regenerate [GAP-14: ...] and [GAP-15: ...] they too that occur [GAP-16: ...] they shall be destroyed and not be restored, resembling [GAP-17: ... neither] regenerate nor shall they [GAP-18: ...] it [sh]all please him concerning [GAP-19: ...] and grows [GAP-20: ...] in what belongs to evil and the proprium [GAP-21: ...] from him. This selfish will that is corrupt [GAP-22: ...] within the regenerating will and they [GAP-23: ...] are in a state of spiritual infirmity.

*The passage classifies three orders of spiritual perception within the natural mind: those which, like grasses and renewable growths, spring back after being cut away — these are natural knowledges grounded in good; those which, once severed, cannot regenerate — these are deeper perceptions whose interior root has been destroyed; and a third condition, where the corrupt proprium (the selfish will belonging to the old nature) persists within the living, regenerating will, producing a state the teaching calls spiritual sickness — an incomplete regeneration in which evil and good coexist painfully in the same mind.*

reconstructions.reconstructed_text: why when limbs are cut from the body of the person he shall be pained? While if the hair on the head of the person's body should be shaved, and [the nai]ls of his hands and feet be cut, he does not notice it [nor feel pain] Some of these even now shall grow an[d come forth] again. Just as the na[ils are cut and grow] so the hair shall grow and [if you] cut a finger, he in [deed is pained] on the limbs of the [bod]y that you [cut from] him [shall not grow] since this time to the [dissolution of] the body ag[a]in.

th[at the] body is like the earth, wh[ile these] limbs als[o growing out] of it are like the trees. There are varieties [and kinds] of tree you shall find growing on the earth. They ar[is]e and grow again and stand firm. They have not [been uprooted from the earth] Again, there are others that if they are cut shall not [grow again] and they grow, as they are li[ke the grass] which shall be cut and grow [again] and [again] they too that occur [on the earth] they shall be cut and not grow, resembling [the limbs that shall neither] grow nor shall they [grow again. And] it [sh]all please him on [that which is cut] and grows [again] in impurity [and shall not be cut away] from him. This flesh that is corrupt [is mingled] in the liv[in]g flesh and they [in whom it dwells] are somewhat sick.

fills.explanation: The chapter's guiding question is about pain vs. no pain; after "he does not notice it," the text naturally completes the contrast by adding that he also feels no pain, matching the spiritual sense of not perceiving loss.
Completing "and come forth again" — the outermost forms (hair/nails) regenerate by coming forth anew, matching the spiritual sense of ultimate forms re-emerging because their root remains intact.
Completing "nails are cut and grow" to form the first half of the simile: "Just as the nails are cut and grow, so the hair shall grow" — both ultimate forms regenerate after removal.

Introduces the conditional contrast: after describing things that regrow, the text shifts to "if you cut a finger" — an essential faculty that does NOT regrow — matching the spiritual transition to severing a living faculty.

Completes "he indeed is pained" — when an essential faculty (finger/limb) is severed, the person suffers real pain, matching the spiritual sense that destruction of interior faculties occasions genuine suffering.
Completes "the limbs of the body that you cut from him" — the natural-register expression for severing essential faculties from the person, matching the chapter's cutting imagery throughout.

The main predicate for the relative clause about cut limbs: "the limbs that you cut from him shall not grow since this time" — essential faculties once destroyed cannot regenerate, unlike the outermost forms.

Completes "since this time to the dissolution of the body again" — the severed limbs will not regrow for the remainder of the body's existence, matching the spiritual sense that destroyed interior faculties are lost until the natural mind is dissolved.

Completes "also growing out of it" — the limbs growing out of the body correspond to trees growing out of the earth, matching the spiritual sense of faculties rooted in the natural mind as ground of reception.
Standard Kephalaia doublet "varieties and kinds" to express the diverse orders of perception/trees growing in the natural mind/earth.

The first class of trees regrow because their root remains intact; "they have not been uprooted from the earth" expresses why they stand firm — their spiritual root in the ground of reception is undisturbed.
Completes "shall not grow again" for the second class of trees/perceptions that once cut cannot be restored, matching the spiritual sense of deeper faculties whose interior root has been destroyed.
Completes "like the grass" — grass is the natural correspondence for outermost knowledges that spring back when cut, forming the renewable class of perceptions in the analogy's third category.
Completes "shall be cut and grow again" — the defining characteristic of the grass-like class is its capacity to regenerate after being cut, directly paralleling the hair and nails from ¶2.
Discourse marker "and again" introducing the next category in the classification sequence, a standard Kephalaia transitional formula for enumerating successive classes.
Completes "they too that occur on the earth" — maintaining the governing analogy of the body as earth, locating this final class of non-regrowing growths on the ground of reception.

Completes "resembling the limbs that shall neither grow" — the non-regrowing trees are explicitly compared back to the bodily limbs from ¶2, closing the correspondential circle between earth-analogy and body-analogy.
Completes the clause about non-regrowing limbs ("nor shall they grow again") and transitions with "And" to the new topic of what grows in impurity — the corrupt flesh that persists within the living.

Completes "it shall please him on that which is cut and grows" — introducing the paradoxical case where something cut away still grows back, but now in impurity, corresponding to the corrupt proprium that regenerates in evil.

Completes "and grows again in impurity" — the corrupt flesh/proprium keeps returning even after being cut, but its regrowth is in impurity rather than in good, matching the spiritual sense of evil regenerating within the natural mind.

fills.fill: and shall not be cut away
fills.explanation: The corrupt growth in impurity cannot be fully separated from the person — matching the spiritual sense that the old proprium persists inseparably within the natural mind during incomplete regeneration.

Completes "This flesh that is corrupt is mingled in the living flesh" — the corrupt will is intermixed with the regenerating will, expressing Swedenborg's teaching on the coexistence of the old and new will during incomplete regeneration.

Completes "and they in whom it dwells are somewhat sick" — those in whom the corrupt flesh persists within the living flesh experience spiritual infirmity, the state of incomplete regeneration where evil and good coexist painfully.
